rule_set: Rule set applied: the site’s six structural rules S1–S6 (model.json v1.0.0), a CSSCPSG reading of each sentence’s actor, act, object and scope.

rules.S1: Scope: the operative noun phrase covers more (or other) land than the instrument it rests on evidences
rules.S2: Party: the person most affected is not a party, not the addressee, or not shown to have been served
rules.S3: Agency: the operative effect is imposed without any act or consent of the person it binds
rules.S4: Term shift: a key word (possession, owner, proprietor, possessions) changes meaning between documents
rules.S5: Text gap: the operative text is known only from a later recital or summary
rules.S6: Inconsistency: dates, years or descriptions conflict between records of the same act

note: Verbatim passages; red marks are additions only. Paragraph numbers count the BAILII text.

passages.src: Surrender and new yearly tenancy, as recited by the Court of Appeal
passages.cite: BP Properties Ltd v Buckler [1987] EWCA Civ 2, Court of Appeal, 31 July 1987, Dillon LJ, BAILII text ¶5
passages.text: It appears that Mr Williams, who may already by then have been elderly, fell into arrears with his rent in the mid-1930s and in the late 1940s. Because of that, agreement was reached for Mr Williams' tenancy to be surrendered and for a new yearly agricultural tenancy commencing at February 2 1949 to be granted to Mr Williams' son-in-law, Mr Frederick Buckler, who was the father of Mr Buckler junior. It was intended that Mr Frederick Buckler should have a written tenancy agreement, but this did not happen because Mr Frederick Buckler also failed to pay the rent. There is a letter from the landlords' agents to their solicitors of October 10 1952 stating that they did not propose to proceed with the letting to Mr Frederick Buckler. However, the conclusion must be that, even though there was no written agreement, Mr Frederick Buckler had a periodic tenancy which was protected by the Agricultural Holdings Act.

marks.p: even though there was no written agreement
marks.why: No written tenancy exists for 1949. Its terms and its land are known only from this later recital.

marks.p: It appears that
marks.why: The recital opens on inference. The rent books and the agents’ letter of 10 October 1952 are not quoted.

passages.src: High Court possession order under Order 14, as recited by the Court of Appeal (EV-0032)
passages.cite: BP Properties Ltd v Buckler [1987] EWCA Civ 2, Court of Appeal, 31 July 1987, Dillon LJ, BAILII text ¶6
passages.text: His tenancy was then duly terminated by a notice to quit which expired on February 2 1955. Western Ground Rents then brought proceedings for possession against Mr Frederick Buckler in the High Court and obtained a possession order, under Order 14, in respect of the whole of the farm. On July 4 1955 that possession order was enforced, and possession was taken in respect of all parts of the farm except the farmhouse and garden. The reason why the order was not enforced in respect of the farmhouse and garden was that Mrs Mary Buckler (daughter of Mr Williams, wife of Mr Frederick Buckler and mother of Mr Buckler junior) had recently come out of hospital after having had a leg amputated and was objecting very strongly to leaving the farmhouse.

marks.p: against Mr Frederick Buckler
marks.why: The order was sought against the tenant alone. Mary (Nancy) Williams lived in the farmhouse and was not a party.

marks.p: in respect of the whole of the farm
marks.why: The order is recited as covering the whole farm. No plan or parcel list is quoted.

marks.p: all parts of the farm except the farmhouse and garden
marks.why: The enforced area is described by exclusion only. No plan defines the parts taken on 4 July 1955.

passages.src: Cardiff County Court possession order, as recited by the Court of Appeal
passages.cite: BP Properties Ltd v Buckler [1987] EWCA Civ 2, Court of Appeal, 31 July 1987, Dillon LJ, BAILII text ¶9
passages.text: In 1962, however, Western Ground Rents brought a fresh action in Cardiff County Court against Mr Frederick Buckler and Mrs Buckler for possession of the farmhouse and garden and mesne profits since 1955. On December 11 1962 a possession order was made by Judge Temple Morris QC together with an order for payment of mesne profits. The latter was to some extent enforced, in that there seems to have been a suspended committal order against Mr Frederick Buckler in June 1963, but nothing was done before 1974 to enforce the 1962 possession order.

passages.src: BP Pension Trust Ltd v Mrs Buckler, Cardiff County Court, as recited by the Court of Appeal
passages.cite: BP Properties Ltd v Buckler [1987] EWCA Civ 2, Court of Appeal, 31 July 1987, Dillon LJ, BAILII text ¶11
passages.text: In 1974 BP Pension Trust Ltd started a fresh action in the Cardiff County Court for possession and mesne profits against Mrs Buckler (sued as Mrs Williams) and various members of her family, including Mr Buckler junior. This was adjourned part heard on July 3 1974 for a formal defence to be filed on behalf of Mrs Buckler, and a defence was filed asserting that BP Pension Trust's claim was barred by adverse possession under the Limitation Act 1939; so far as Mr Buckler junior is concerned, it was pleaded that he occupied the property as licensee of Mrs Buckler. That action has never been finally heard. However, on September 17 1974 BP Pension Trust Ltd gave notice of an application by them as successors in title to Western Ground Rents for leave to enforce the possession order of December 11 1962 (the order of Judge Temple Morris QC) and on September 19 1974 Judge Watkin Powell on that application gave BP Pension Trust Ltd leave to execute the order for possession of December 11 1962. He ordered that the possession warrant do issue forthwith but be not enforced until October 31 1974.

marks.p: as successors in title to Western Ground Rents
marks.why: Leave to enforce rested on succession to the 1962 judgment. The deed that made BP Pension Trust the successor is not on either first-registration file.

passages.src: Letter, BP Pension Trust Ltd to Mrs Buckler, as quoted by the Court of Appeal
passages.cite: BP Properties Ltd v Buckler [1987] EWCA Civ 2, Court of Appeal, 31 July 1987, Dillon LJ, BAILII text ¶15
passages.text: We have been advised that you are making an application to the Court for a Stay of Execution of the Order for Possession which was recently confirmed, and that you are proposing to apply to have the judgment of the Court, which we were seeking to enforce, set aside. You will, we hope, understand that the Trustees of The British Petroleum Pension Trust are not, and never have been, unsympathetic to your position, but they are bound in law to have a prime regard for the interests of their Pensioners and they had no alternative but to exercise remedies against you which the law provides. The only way in which they could safeguard your future occupation of Great House Farm is by selling the property to a purchaser who is not bound by similar constraints. We are now pleased to advise you that we have found such a purchaser in BP Properties Ltd, who have agreed to buy the property from the Trust. Accordingly, the instructions given to the Bailiff to execute the judgment of the Court have been withdrawn. As the Possession Order will not now be executed, your application for a Stay of Execution becomes unnecessary. Your Solicitors are immediately being advised accordingly.

marks.p: who have agreed to buy the property from the Trust
marks.why: No written agreement of this date is held. HM Land Registry lists a plan to the conveyance dated 23 February 1975, almost four months later.

passages.src: Letter, BP Properties Ltd to Mrs Buckler, as quoted by the Court of Appeal
passages.cite: BP Properties Ltd v Buckler [1987] EWCA Civ 2, Court of Appeal, 31 July 1987, Dillon LJ, BAILII text ¶16
passages.text: You will be hearing separately from our Pension Trust that they are selling Great House Farm to BP Properties Ltd. As BP Properties is not obliged by the same constraints as the Pension Trust and since we wish to help you as much as possible, we are prepared to allow you to remain in occupation of the house and garden rent free for as long as you may wish and for the rest of your life if you so desire. I am pleased accordingly to confirm that we will not require you to give possession during your lifetime or until such time as you may choose no longer to live in the house, and we have given the necessary instructions so that no proceedings will be commenced until you personally no longer live there. I do hope that by making this gesture you will accept the situation and that no further problems will arise in the future.

marks.p: we are prepared to allow you to remain in occupation
marks.why: The permission is imposed by the paper owner without any act or consent of the occupier. It is the sentence the whole judgment rests on.

marks.p: they are selling Great House Farm to BP Properties Ltd
marks.why: The sale is stated as present fact. The conveyance to BP Properties Ltd is dated 23 May 1975.

passages.src: Hearing and withdrawal of the warrant, as recited by the Court of Appeal
passages.cite: BP Properties Ltd v Buckler [1987] EWCA Civ 2, Court of Appeal, 31 July 1987, Dillon LJ, BAILII text ¶13; ¶16
passages.text: Both are addressed to Mrs Buckler (described again as Mrs Williams), but both were in fact sent not to her but to her solicitor, who seems to have received them on the morning of November 4, immediately before he made his application to Judge Watkin Powell in the Cardiff County Court. Because of these two letters the landlords' solicitors did not attend the appointment before the judge on November 4 1974. Mrs Buckler's solicitors produced the letters to the judge, and he stayed execution on the warrant for possession pending Mrs Buckler's agreement to the proposals in the letters. Her solicitor then telephoned Mrs Buckler, told her of the letters and sought her instructions. Before she had given any instructions, however, the landlords' solicitors themselves wrote to the county court, at some date prior to November 25 1974 and withdrew the warrant for possession. Mrs Buckler therefore never expressly accepted or rejected the terms of the two letters. She was left in undisturbed possession of the farmhouse and garden, rent free, until her death, which occurred in March 1983.

marks.p: sent not to her but to her solicitor
marks.why: The letters were addressed to Mrs Buckler but delivered to her solicitor. The person bound by the licence did not receive it.
marks.ev: BP Properties Ltd v Buckler [1987] EWCA Civ 2, Court of Appeal, 31 July 1987, Dillon LJ, BAILII text ¶13

marks.p: pending Mrs Buckler's agreement to the proposals in the letters
marks.why: The court stayed execution pending her agreement. The warrant was then withdrawn before she gave any.

marks.p: never expressly accepted or rejected
marks.why: The record shows no act of hers either way. The licence still bound her.

marks.why: The decision dates the family’s occupancy from 1916. Trade directories list John Williams at Great House from 1868; 1916 is the date of the tenancy the judgment recites.

passages.src: Judgment of Hollis J (Queen’s Bench Division, Cardiff), as recited by the Court of Appeal
passages.cite: BP Properties Ltd v Buckler [1987] EWCA Civ 2, Court of Appeal, 31 July 1987, Dillon LJ, BAILII text ¶23
passages.text: The judge rejected the primary claim on the ground that Mr Frederick Buckler's possession during his lifetime was not 'adverse', and so time did not begin to run against the landlords until after his death. On the second argument he held that the effect of the letters of October 31 1974 was to constitute Mrs Buckler the licensee of BP Properties Ltd, and thus no longer in adverse possession, even though the letters were written unilaterally and without any agreement with her. The defence under the 1939 and 1980 Acts therefore failed.

marks.p: even though the letters were written unilaterally and without any agreement with her
marks.why: The trial judge held the licence effective with no agreement from the person it bound.

passages.text: 'no person shall be deemed to have been in possession of any land by reason only of having made a formal entry thereon, and no continual or other claim upon or near any land shall preserve any right of action to recover the land'.

passages.src: Court of Appeal: the enforcement point
passages.cite: BP Properties Ltd v Buckler [1987] EWCA Civ 2, Court of Appeal, 31 July 1987, Dillon LJ, BAILII text ¶32
passages.text: It follows that enforcement of the judgment for possession of December 11 1962 was still open to the landlords at October 31 1974, and their title to the farmhouse and garden had not been extinguished. I would accordingly reject the contention that Mrs Buckler had acquired a title by adverse possession before October 31 1974.

marks.p: was still open to the landlords
marks.why: The 1962 order was made for Western Ground Rents. Its transfer to BP Pension Trust rests on the 1969 sale, which is not on either first-registration file.

passages.src: Court of Appeal: the "wrong company" argument
passages.cite: BP Properties Ltd v Buckler [1987] EWCA Civ 2, Court of Appeal, 31 July 1987, Dillon LJ, BAILII text ¶22
passages.text: I see nothing in this rather technical point; the letters record sufficiently that BP Properties Ltd had agreed to buy the property from the Pension Trust, and BP Properties Ltd was therefore prima facie in a position to grant a licence to Mrs Buckler.

marks.p: the letters record sufficiently that BP Properties Ltd had agreed to buy
marks.why: The agreement itself was not before the court. Its existence rests on the words of the letters alone.

passages.src: Court of Appeal: repudiation
passages.cite: BP Properties Ltd v Buckler [1987] EWCA Civ 2, Court of Appeal, 31 July 1987, Dillon LJ, BAILII text ¶38
passages.text: It may be that the result would have been different if Mrs Buckler had, as soon as she learned of the letters, plainly told BP Properties Ltd that she did not accept the letters, and maintained her claims to be already the owner of the property; she did not, however, do that.

marks.p: she did not, however, do that
marks.why: The finding places the burden of rejection on the occupier. Her silence becomes consent to a licence she never asked for.

passages.src: Court of Appeal: the licence
passages.cite: BP Properties Ltd v Buckler [1987] EWCA Civ 2, Court of Appeal, 31 July 1987, Dillon LJ, BAILII text ¶40–41
passages.text: The nature of Mrs Buckler's possession after receipt of the letters cannot be decided just by looking at what was locked up in her own mind. It must depend even more, on this aspect of the case, on the position as seen from the standpoint of the person with the paper title. What could that person have done? The rule that possession is not adverse if it can be referred to a lawful title applies even if the person in possession did not know of the lawful title; the lawful title would still preclude the person with the paper title from evicting the person in possession. So far as Mrs Buckler was concerned, even though she did not 'accept' the terms of the letters, BP Properties Ltd would, in the absence of any repudiation by her of the two letters, have been bound to treat her as in possession as licensee on the terms of the letters. They could not have evicted her (if they could have done so at all) without determining the licence. I can see no escape therefore from the conclusion that, whether she liked it or not, from the time of her receipt of the letters, Mrs Buckler was in possession of the farmhouse and garden by the licence of BP Properties Ltd, and her possession was no longer adverse within the meaning of section 10 of the 1939 Act.

marks.p: cannot be decided just by looking at what was locked up in her own mind
marks.why: The occupier’s intention is set aside for the owner’s standpoint. The Law Commission later called this assumption discredited.

marks.p: whether she liked it or not
marks.why: The licence binds her without her act or consent.

marks.p: by the licence of BP Properties Ltd
marks.why: On 31 October 1974 BP Properties Ltd did not hold the title. Its conveyance is dated 23 May 1975.

passages.src: European Commission of Human Rights: Article 8 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1
passages.cite: European Commission of Human Rights, Decision as to the admissibility of Application No. 14464/88, 14 April 1989, The Law, paras 2–3, pp. 3–4
passages.text: The Commission notes that the applicant has lived in the property in question since his birth and that the decision of the court giving possession to B.P. (Properties) Ltd could be considered as an interference with the applicant's right to respect for his home. The Commission finds however that the order, pursuant to court proceedings, was in accordance with law and was "necessary in a democratic society" for the legitimate aim of protecting the rights of 14464/88 ■r 4 - Other, namely, the rights of B.P. (Properties) Ltd, who were held to be owner of the property. The Commission accordingly finds any interference justified within the meaning of Article 8 para. 2 of the Convention. It follows that this complaint is manifestly ill-founded within the meaning of Article 27 para. 2 of the Convention. 3. The applicant has complained that the decisions have interfered within his rights under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention, which provides: "Every natural or legal person is entitled to the peaceful enjoyment of his possessions. No one shall be deprived of his possessions except in the public interest and subject to the conditions provided for by law and by the general principles of international law. The preceding provisions shall not, however, in any way impair the right of a State to enforce such laws as it deems necessary to control the use of property in accordance with the general interest or to secure the payment of taxes or other contributions or penalties." The Commission recalls however that the courts held that the applicant had no right to occupy the property, which belonged to another. The Commission finds, therefore, that there has been no interference with the applicant's possessions within the meaning of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1..

marks.p: who were held to be owner of the property
marks.why: The domestic courts decided possession under a licence. The Commission restates that as ownership.
marks.ev: BP Properties Ltd v Buckler [1987] EWCA Civ 2, Court of Appeal, 31 July 1987, Dillon LJ, BAILII text ¶40

marks.p: which belonged to another
marks.why: The word turns a possession ruling into a title finding. No court quoted the 1938 conveyance or its plan.
